narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 79.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by how your academic performance compared with students who are typically admitted. Your class ranking at the end of your first year and again at the end of your third year were the two strongest factors. In both cases, your standing placed you at the very bottom of your cohort—far below the average ranking of about 6 among accepted students. These unusually low rankings strongly pushed the model toward expecting bar exam failure.

Your family income bracket was the third most important factor. Being from an upper-middle-income background actually worked slightly in your favor, since that bracket is common among successful applicants. However, this modest positive influence was not nearly enough to offset the much larger negative effect of your academic rankings.

Your LSAT score of 29 and undergraduate GPA of 2.9 were also below the averages of accepted students (37 and 3.23 respectively), reinforcing the same pattern.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Once you have clearer evidence of stronger performance, reapply. Many students successfully gain admission on a second attempt after addressing these exact gaps.
